To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
feeding attenuated the expression of genes that promote protein degradation, but did not enhance protein synthesis in response to a bout of aerobic exercise.
a nonexhausitive bout of aerobic exercise stimulated skeletal muscle FSR and that feeding attenuated the expression of genes regulating protein degradation and myogenesis.
a nonexhausitve bout of exercise stimulates mixed-muscle protein synthesis, and feeding does not further increase mixed-muscle FSR between 1 and 2 hours after the cessation of exercise.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of aerobic exercise on muscle protein turnover in the fed and fasted states.
the effects of exercise, diet and nutrition and their interactions on the regulation of muscle mass and strength.
the regulation of muscle protein synthesis and gene transcription in the fasted versus fed state after aerobic exercise.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ingestion of a carbohydrate and protein beverage after aerobic exercise attenuates muscle proteolysis and does not alter FSR in the postexercise period.

a single meal of 5 kcal/kg body wt consumed 60 min after a nonexhausting bout of aerobic exercise attenuates the expression, but not the activation, of factors that regulate muscle protein degradation and does not enhance muscle protein synthesis.
feeding after aerobic exercise does not enhance the stimulation of muscle protein synthesis and that feeding after aerobic activity does not alter muscle protein degradation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ingestion of carbohydrate and protein after aerobic exercise does not further enhance muscle protein synthesis and attenuates the expression factors involved in muscle protein degradation.
the ingestion of carbohydrate and protein after an aerobic exercise bout does not increase the rate of muscle protein synthesis, but does attenuate the upregulation of proteolytic genes.
the postexercise feeding of 5 kcal·kg body wt(-1) does not enhance muscle protein synthesis but attenuates the expression levels of proteolytic proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a bout of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise can increase the rate of muscle protein synthesis, but this response is attenuated by feeding.
feeding does not enhance the muscle protein synthetic response to aerobic exercise.
a nonexercised fasted individual is not likely to have a greater rate of muscle protein synthesis than a fasted individual who has just exercised.
